messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marta Kovač had spent much of her adult life in the cockpit, a combat pilot who trusted procedures, altitude, and disciplined attention more than comfort or rest. The bombing at the transit terminal happened on a brief layover while she was traveling for training, in a crowded concourse where the sudden concussion of the blast turned ordinary noise into a rupture. One moment she had been moving with the flow of bodies and luggage; the next she was on the floor, ears ringing, tasting dust and smoke, with people shouting, stumbling, and grabbing at one another in the crush. In the months afterward, the world narrowed around the moments that most resembled that day. When Marta felt physically unwell—lightheaded, nauseated, or simply “off”—it brought back the same jolt of alarm she had felt before the blast and she would reach for a cigarette to steady herself, telling herself she needed something to cut through the feeling. Loud noises worked on her in the same way: a slamming hangar door, an unexpected backfire, even the sharp crack of equipment in the briefing room could send her heart racing and leave her scanning for an exit. Crowded places were worse still. In terminals, grocery aisles, and the packed training cafeteria, she felt herself tightening, counting heads, studying faces, and looking for gaps in the crowd where she could move if something happened. She had come to believe that these reactions were proof of what she feared most—that the world was a dangerous place and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. Even small disruptions, like a delayed flight or a change in schedule, felt intolerable to her now; she was certain she could not deal with even the slightest upset, and that conviction made her reach for familiar routines, cigarettes, and her blunt private refrain that it could have been worse.

That belief settled in alongside a more corrosive one: if she was already this fragile, then any sudden sound, illness, or crowd might be the beginning of another catastrophe. Marta began to watch herself and the world for signs of threat, moving through her day superalert and constantly checking behind her when she walked to her car or crossed open tarmac. Her sleep deteriorated because she lay awake listening for noises and replaying routes, exits, and who had stood too close to her in public spaces. The more she stayed on guard, the more she noticed every loud clang, every press of bodies, every odd sensation in her chest or stomach, and those sensations in turn confirmed her sense that danger was close. She avoided enclosed or confined spaces whenever she could, taking stairs instead of elevators and standing near doors in meeting rooms, because being boxed in made her feel trapped and helpless, like she would not be able to stop anything once it started. At work, this had begun to affect her functioning in ways she could not ignore: she passed on certain travel assignments, arrived early to avoid crowded transport, and chose seats and routes with an almost ritual precision. She still told herself, in a flat and practiced way, that it could have been worse, but the sentence no longer comforted her for long. It only seemed to make the danger feel more permanent, as if survival itself had been narrow enough to prove how little control she truly had.

Over time, Marta’s attempts to manage her distress kept feeding the same cycle. Smoking became a quick answer whenever a memory, a physical sensation, or the press of people unsettled her, and though it gave her a few moments of relief, it also left her more keyed up and more alert to every internal shift. The cigarette breaks became a way to escape the briefing room, the crowded cafeteria, and any enclosed space that made her feel boxed in, but each escape reinforced the sense that those situations were too dangerous to tolerate. When she noticed herself growing frightened of ordinary discomforts, she would repeat that it could have been worse, trying to outrun the memory by comparing it to the deadlier possibilities she had witnessed on television and in reports, yet the comparison only deepened her impression that catastrophe could erupt again at any moment. Her hypervigilance kept bringing her back to the same triggers: a cough in a queue, a metallic bang in the hangar, the sudden weakness of feeling ill after too little sleep. Each one made her check behind her, scan faces, and seek the nearest door. By the time she sought help, Marta was exhausted, sleeping badly, smoking more than she wanted, and increasingly isolated at work and in her personal life. What finally brought her in was the fear that the tightening circle of watchfulness, avoidance, and dread was shrinking her world as surely as the blast had once shattered the terminal. She did not want to feel trapped by crowds, noises, or her own body anymore, but what she feared most was that she would never again trust herself to keep disaster from finding her.
